b: Today about 2.3 to 2.4 billion people, roughly three in ten of the world's population, identify as Christians, which makes it the largest religion in the world. The story of the last century is a story of change in the shape of the church. In 1910 about two out of three Christians lived in Europe. A hundred years later fewer than three in ten did. The center of gravity has moved south and east.

Sub-Saharan Africa now has one of the largest Christian populations of any region, growing from about nine million in 1910 to hundreds of millions today. Latin America is home to a large share of the world's Catholics. In Asia, Christianity is growing fast in places such as South Korea, where roughly a quarter to a third of the people are Christian, and in China, where the number of Protestants is estimated at several tens of millions and much of the growth takes place in house churches outside state control. Meanwhile, in Europe and in parts of North America, church attendance has declined.

The face of the church is changing. The typical Christian today is not a white European but is more likely to be a young woman in Nigeria, Brazil or the Philippines. Worship is in thousands of languages. The Bible, in whole or in part, has been translated into over 3,000 languages, with the work of Bible translators continuing in many more.

This is a long way from a small group of Galilean fishermen, and yet John's vision in Revelation, of a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language standing before the throne, is the goal of the story from Genesis 12. The task of every generation is to hand on the faith to the next, and no generation has been left without a witness.

Alexandria in Egypt was the second city of the empire, famous for its library and its scholars, and by the late second century it had become a center of Christian learning. The catechetical school there tried to show that the faith could be taught with the best learning of the age.

Clement of Alexandria, who taught there around AD 190 to 200, argued that Greek philosophy had been a schoolmaster to bring the Greeks to Christ, in the way that the law had been for the Jews. Origen, his greatest student, was the most gifted scholar of the early church. Born around AD 185, he had a father who was killed in a persecution, and as a teenager he wanted to go to martyrdom himself and was stopped only because his mother hid his clothes. He taught from the age of eighteen and wrote on a huge scale.

His Hexapla set six versions of the Old Testament side by side, in Hebrew, in Hebrew letters transliterated into Greek, and in four Greek translations, the earliest serious work in textual criticism. He wrote commentaries on most books of the Bible and a great work of theology, On First Principles. He taught that Scripture has several levels of meaning, literal, moral and spiritual, a method of interpretation that influenced centuries of readers. Some of his speculations were later condemned, including that souls existed before bodies and that all might finally be saved.

During the persecution of Decius in AD 250 he was imprisoned and tortured, and he died not long afterward, about AD 253. Even those who rejected parts of his thought honored his learning. His example showed that the faith can ask hard questions and give honest answers, and also that a gifted mind can wander beyond what the church accepted.

Augustine of Hippo is one of the most influential thinkers in the history of Christianity, in both the Catholic and Protestant traditions. Born in AD 354 in Thagaste, in North Africa, to a pagan father and a devoted Christian mother, Monica, he became a brilliant teacher of rhetoric. For years he pursued pleasure, ambition and the sect of the Manichees. He lived with a woman for about fifteen years and had a son with her.

His conversion is told in his Confessions, written around AD 397 to 400, the first great spiritual autobiography. In a garden in Milan in 386, he heard a child's voice say "Take up and read," and opened the Bible to Romans 13, which told him to put on the Lord Jesus Christ and give up the desires of the flesh. He was baptized by Ambrose the following Easter. The Confessions opens with a line that has been quoted ever since: "You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you."

He became bishop of Hippo in AD 395 and served until his death in 430, while the Vandals were besieging his city. His works are vast. In response to the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410, he wrote The City of God, arguing that earthly empires rise and fall, while the city of God endures. In the controversy with Pelagius, he insisted on the priority of God's grace in salvation, which led him to his teachings on original sin and predestination. His writings on the Trinity, on time and on the nature of the church shaped the Middle Ages.

Luther and Calvin both counted themselves as Augustine's followers, and so do many Catholics. He is a reminder that the greatest theology often comes out of a struggle, and that the one who writes about grace is the one who needed it most.

In 1933 Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany, and many in the Protestant churches welcomed him. A group of pastors and laity, called the German Christians, tried to bring the church into line with Nazi ideas, including the exclusion of Christians of Jewish descent. A minority resisted. In 1934 they met at Barmen and issued a declaration, written mainly by Karl Barth, which said that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God that Christians must hear and obey, and that no other power, state or leader may claim their ultimate loyalty. They became known as the Confessing Church.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a young theologian, born in 1906, who joined the resistance from the first. He warned against the cult of the Führer in a radio talk two days after Hitler became chancellor, and he ran an illegal seminary for the Confessing Church at Finkenwalde. His book The Cost of Discipleship, published in 1937, distinguished "cheap grace," forgiveness without repentance, from "costly grace," which calls us to follow Christ. He was offered a safe place in New York in 1939 but chose to return to Germany.

Eventually he joined a conspiracy that planned to remove Hitler, which was a painful moral decision for a man committed to peace. He was arrested in April 1943, held in prison for two years, and executed on 9 April 1945 at Flossenbürg, a few weeks before the war ended. His letters from prison, published as Letters and Papers from Prison, are still read widely.

Bonhoeffer's story is held up as an example of costly discipleship, and also as a warning of what happens when the church is silent. Many German Christians went along with evil, and others resisted at great cost. His own words from The Cost of Discipleship are often quoted: "When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die."

After Nicaea affirmed that Christ is God, the next question was how his divinity and humanity fit together. At the Council of Ephesus in AD 431, the church condemned Nestorius, the patriarch of Constantinople, whose teaching seemed to divide Christ into two persons, and affirmed that Mary can be called Theotokos, "God-bearer," not to exalt her but to protect the truth that her son was truly God.

Then came an opposite error, held by Eutyches, who said that after the union Christ had only one nature, a blend of divine and human. In AD 451 the emperor called a council in Chalcedon, a city across the strait from Constantinople. About 500 bishops attended. They accepted a letter from Pope Leo of Rome, called the Tome of Leo, and issued a definition of faith: Christ is one person in two natures, "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation."

Not everyone accepted it. Many Christians in Egypt, Syria and Armenia held that Chalcedon had gone too far in dividing the natures and followed the teaching of Cyril of Alexandria, "one incarnate nature of the Word." The churches that rejected the council, today called the Oriental Orthodox churches, include the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches. In recent decades theologians in these churches and the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches have reached agreements that say the differences were largely a matter of words.

Alongside them stood another ancient church, called the Church of the East, which was condemned along with Nestorius and carried Christianity across Persia, India and Central Asia, and even to China by the seventh century. The map of the churches today still shows the lines drawn in the fifth century, which is a good reason to take them seriously.

In AD 312 Constantine, a general fighting for control of the western half of the Roman Empire, marched on Rome to face his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. Christian writers of the time, including Eusebius and Lactantius, report that he had a vision or dream beforehand that told him to put the sign of Christ on his soldiers' shields. He won the battle. In the following year he and the eastern emperor Licinius agreed on a policy, usually called the Edict of Milan, that granted Christians and everyone else freedom to worship.

The change was enormous. Churches that had been meeting in houses began to build great basilicas. Property seized in the persecutions was returned. Constantine gave money to the clergy, exempted them from certain taxes and made Sunday a day of rest. In AD 330 he dedicated a new capital on the Bosporus, Constantinople, which was designed as a Christian city. He was not baptized until shortly before his death in AD 337, a delay not unusual at the time, and historians still argue about how deep his faith was.

The blessings were real, and so were the dangers. Once the emperor favored the church, the church had to deal with the temptation of power. Bishops became important public figures. People joined for advantage as well as conviction. And the emperor, who thought of himself as a kind of overseer of the church, took an interest in settling its quarrels, which led directly to the Council of Nicaea.

Later Christians have weighed this period very differently. Some see it as the triumph of the gospel, and others as the start of a long entanglement of church and state. Both can be true. After Constantine, Christianity was no longer a movement that might get you killed, and by the end of the century it was the empire's official religion.

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries new currents of thought challenged the church in the West. The Enlightenment elevated human reason, and many scholars began to question miracles and the authority of the Bible. Friedrich Schleiermacher, a German pastor and professor who died in 1834, tried to answer the skeptics by defining religion as a feeling of dependence on God, and he is called the father of liberal theology. German scholars applied the methods of historical criticism to the Bible, asking about sources and dates, and at times concluded that large parts of it were not what they claimed to be.

Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, which raised new questions about how to understand Genesis. Some Christians welcomed the theory of evolution and others resisted it. The debates grew bitter, and a conservative reaction took shape. Between 1910 and 1915 a series of twelve booklets called The Fundamentals, financed by two California businessmen, set out the essential doctrines, including the inspiration of Scripture, the virgin birth, the atonement and the resurrection. Those who held them were called fundamentalists. The Scopes trial of 1925, over the teaching of evolution in Tennessee, made them objects of ridicule in the press, though the trial settled little.

The twentieth century brought other responses. The Swiss theologian Karl Barth, shocked by the support of liberal theologians for the German war effort in 1914, published a commentary on Romans in 1919 that stressed the sovereignty and otherness of God and began what was called neo-orthodoxy. Evangelicals, such as Billy Graham, carried on the conservative tradition in a more open way. Many Catholic scholars also joined the work of critical study.

Today Christians still disagree about how far to use historical criticism and how to relate Genesis and science. The good that came from it was that the church had to ask hard questions, and that faith that cannot take questions is not strong. The Bible's own advice is to test everything and hold to what is good.

The English Reformation started for political reasons. When Pope Clement VII would not annul Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, making the king head of the Church of England. But beneath the politics were real reformers.

William Tyndale was a scholar who wanted every English plowboy to know the Scriptures better than the clergy. When the church forbade English translations, he left for the Continent, and in 1526 his New Testament was printed at Worms and smuggled into England in bales of cloth. He had begun translating the Old Testament from the Hebrew when he was betrayed, arrested near Brussels and, in October 1536, strangled and burned. His reported last words were a prayer, "Lord, open the king of England's eyes." Within three years, the king had authorized an English Bible, the Great Bible of 1539, much of it from Tyndale's work.

Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533, gave the church the Book of Common Prayer in 1549 and a revised one in 1552, in beautiful English that shaped the country's worship and speech. When the Catholic queen Mary took the throne in 1553, she restored the old faith and burned about 280 Protestants, including Cranmer in 1556, who held his right hand in the flames because it had signed a recantation. Mary's half-sister Elizabeth came to the throne in 1558, and the Elizabethan settlement of 1559 set up a church that was Protestant in doctrine and kept bishops and a liturgy.

The result was a church of the nation, which was a compromise that satisfied no one entirely. Some wanted further reform and were called Puritans. Others held on to the older ways. The tensions of that settlement would shape English and American history for centuries.

In the high Middle Ages the universities of Europe produced a new kind of theology, in which the church's teaching was explored with rigorous reasoning. It is called scholasticism, and two of its greatest minds were Anselm and Thomas Aquinas.

Anselm, born in Italy about 1033, became a monk in Normandy and later Archbishop of Canterbury. He described his method as "faith seeking understanding," beginning with belief and then asking why it is so. In his Proslogion he offered a famous argument for God's existence, now called the ontological argument, which says that God is "that than which nothing greater can be conceived," and that such a being must exist in reality, not only in thought. His Cur Deus Homo, "Why God Became Man," argued that the offense of sin against God's honor required satisfaction that only a God-man could make, and it shaped later views of the atonement.

Thomas Aquinas was born around 1225 into a noble family in Italy and joined the Dominicans against his family's wishes. He studied under Albert the Great in Paris and Cologne, and became the most influential theologian of the medieval church. His great work, the Summa Theologiae, written from 1265, treats the whole of Christian doctrine through thousands of carefully argued questions. He drew on Aristotle, whose works had just returned to the West, and held that faith and reason can work together, since both come from the same God.

In December 1273 he stopped writing, after what seems to have been some profound experience at Mass, and told a friend that everything he had written seemed to him like straw compared with what he had seen. He died in 1274 before finishing the Summa. In the Catholic Church he is called the Angelic Doctor. Protestants disagree with him on several points, but his clarity has been admired by almost everyone.

The thirteenth century saw a new kind of religious order. Instead of withdrawing into monasteries, the friars lived among the people, begged for their food and preached in the cities. Two men founded the most influential.

Francis was born about 1181 in Assisi, the son of a rich cloth merchant. As a young man he was a carefree party leader, and then a soldier who was captured and fell ill. While praying in the broken chapel of San Damiano, he heard a voice from the crucifix telling him to rebuild the church. He renounced his inheritance, in a famous scene in the square, and gave himself to poverty. Others joined him, and about 1209 or 1210 Pope Innocent III approved his simple rule. Francis loved all creation and wrote the Canticle of the Sun. In 1224 he is said to have received the stigmata, the marks of Christ's wounds, and he died in 1226.

Dominic, born in Spain about 1170, saw that heresy was spreading in southern France, and decided that the answer was better preaching, by educated men who lived simply. His Order of Preachers, approved in 1216, trained its members in theology and sent them to the universities. Aquinas was a Dominican.

The friars brought the gospel into the new towns, taught and cared for the poor. Their strengths became their weaknesses: Franciscans quarreled about how strict their poverty should be, and some of the orders later became wealthy. But the idea that the church should be among the poor, in simple trust, has returned again and again. Francis' prayer, often attributed to him although it comes from a later time, begins, "Lord, make me an instrument of your peace."
In the second century the church faced its first major internal crisis. Several movements offered a different Christianity, and the way the church responded shaped what it became.

Gnosticism was a family of teachings that promised salvation through secret knowledge, in Greek gnosis. Most Gnostics held that the material world was made by a lesser or even evil being, not the true God, and that the spirit must escape from matter. Some said Christ only seemed to have a body, since a divine being could not be tainted by flesh. Gnostic writings such as the Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of Judas were written in the second century or later, and many were found in the Egyptian desert at Nag Hammadi in 1945. They claim secret teaching from the apostles, but they come long after the apostles.

Marcion, a wealthy shipowner from Pontus who came to Rome about AD 140, went in a different direction. He taught that the God of the Old Testament, a God of law and wrath, was a different God from the Father of Jesus, who is a God of love. He threw out the whole Old Testament and made his own Bible, with an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. The church in Rome expelled him around AD 144.

The church replied in three ways. First, it pointed to the apostolic succession: the churches founded by the apostles had preserved their teaching, and leaders could show how it had been handed down. Second, it formulated a rule of faith, a short summary of the basic beliefs, which grew into the Apostles' Creed. Third, it moved toward a settled canon of Scripture, in part because Marcion had forced the question of which books were authoritative. The danger had led to clarity, as a later lesson on the canon describes.
Two of the greatest early defenders of the faith worked at opposite ends of the Mediterranean, and between them they laid the foundations of orthodox theology.

Irenaeus was born in Asia Minor, where in his youth he heard Polycarp preach, and became bishop of Lyon in Gaul about AD 177. Around AD 180 he wrote Against Heresies, a long refutation of the Gnostics. He argues that the one God made the world through the Word and the Spirit, that matter is good, and that Christ became man to save the whole person. He says that the apostles' teaching has been kept openly in the churches, and he gives a short statement of the faith that is a forerunner of the creeds. He describes the whole story of salvation as a recapitulation, a summing up, in which Christ goes over again the path of Adam and reverses it.

Tertullian was a lawyer from Carthage in North Africa who became a Christian about AD 197 and wrote in Latin. He was the first great Latin theologian, with a sharp pen. He coined many terms that became standard, including the Latin word trinitas, Trinity, and the formula "one substance, three persons." He defended the church against the charge of being a danger to society, and he asked, "What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?", by which he meant that the church did not need Greek philosophy to tell it what to believe. Late in life he drifted into the Montanist movement, which stressed new prophecy and strict discipline, and left the main church.

Both men worked with a conviction that is easy to overlook: that the faith was handed down, and was not invented by each age. Their writings show a church that was already confessing God as Trinity, Christ as divine and human, and the body as part of the redemption.

John Wesley was born in 1703, one of the nineteen children of an Anglican clergyman and his remarkable wife Susanna. At Oxford he and his brother Charles led a group of students who met for prayer, Bible study and charitable work, and were mocked as the Holy Club, or "Methodists," for their methodical habits. Wesley went to Georgia as a missionary in 1735 and returned feeling a failure. "I went to America to convert the Indians," he wrote, "but oh, who shall convert me?"

On 24 May 1738, in a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London, while someone read Luther's preface to Romans, he felt his heart "strangely warmed." He knew that he did trust Christ alone for salvation, and that Christ had taken away his sins. The next year his friend George Whitefield invited him to preach in the open air to coal miners near Bristol, and though he thought it improper at first, he did it. For the next fifty years he rode and walked thousands of miles on horseback, preaching, forming societies and organizing classes for prayer and mutual accountability.

Wesley taught that salvation is for all, that it can be known, and that it leads to holiness of heart and life. He cared for the poor, set up schools and clinics, opposed slavery and wrote on health. His brother Charles wrote thousands of hymns, including "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing" and "O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing."

Wesley never wanted to leave the Church of England, and he died in 1791 still a priest. But after his death the Methodist societies became a separate church. Methodism spread across Britain and especially America, where it became one of the largest Protestant bodies, and it later gave rise to the Holiness and Pentecostal movements.

Martin Luther was born in 1483 in Eisleben, Germany, the son of a miner. He was studying law in 1505 when a violent thunderstorm threw him to the ground, and he cried out a vow to become a monk if he were spared. He entered an Augustinian monastery at Erfurt, where he fasted, confessed for hours and tormented himself over whether he was good enough for God. Later he became a professor of Bible at the new university in Wittenberg, and as he lectured on the Psalms and on Romans, a discovery slowly changed his life. He saw that the righteousness of God in Romans 1:17 was not the standard that condemns but the gift that saves, given to those who trust Christ.

Meanwhile, the church was raising funds for the new St. Peter's Basilica in Rome by selling indulgences, documents that were understood to reduce the time a soul would spend in purgatory. The Dominican preacher Johann Tetzel, who sold them near Wittenberg, was said to use the line "As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs." Luther was alarmed that people thought they could buy forgiveness. According to tradition, on 31 October 1517 he nailed a list of ninety-five theses for debate to the door of the castle church in Wittenberg. Historians doubt the nailing, but they agree that he sent the theses to the archbishop that day.

They were quickly translated and printed, and within weeks they were known across Germany. Luther did not set out to start a new church. He wanted to reform the existing one. But in 1520 the pope threatened him with excommunication, and he burned the bull in public. The reform movement now had a name, and his ideas, justification by faith alone, Scripture alone as the final authority, and the priesthood of all believers, became the heart of Protestantism.
As the western Roman Empire fell apart in the fifth century, Christianity moved into the lands beyond it. A series of missionaries carried the faith to peoples who had never been part of Rome.

Patrick, born in Roman Britain in the early fifth century, was kidnapped at sixteen by Irish raiders and held as a slave, herding sheep for six years. He escaped and returned home, but later had a dream in which the people of Ireland seemed to call him back. He went to Ireland as a bishop and spent the rest of his life preaching and founding churches. His Confession, written in rough Latin, is one of the few writings that survive from this period, and tells of his faith and his struggles.

Irish monasteries then sent their own missionaries. Columba founded a monastery on the island of Iona off Scotland in 563, which became a base for evangelizing the Picts and the north of England. Pope Gregory the Great, who led the church from 590 to 604, sent a monk named Augustine to England, who arrived in Kent in 597 and baptized King Ethelbert. Later Boniface, an English monk, went to Germany in the eighth century. According to his biographer he cut down an oak sacred to the god Thor in about 723, and when nothing happened, many were converted. He was killed by raiders in Frisia in 754.

The missionaries worked slowly, learning languages and winning the rulers. Their churches and monasteries became centers of learning, literacy and care for the poor. In this way, over some six or seven centuries, much of Europe became Christian. The pattern repeats through the history of the church: the faith spreads from the edges as much as from the center.

In the early fourth century a priest in Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son of God was the first and greatest of God's creations, but still a creature. "There was a time when he was not," his followers said. Bishop Alexander of Alexandria disagreed, and the quarrel spread across the Greek-speaking church, until the emperor Constantine, who wanted unity, called the bishops together.

More than 300 bishops met in the city of Nicaea, in what is now Turkey, in AD 325. The council condemned Arius and wrote a creed that confessed Christ as "God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father." The key word was homoousios, "of one substance," which said that the Son shares the Father's very being and is not a lesser being made by him.

The fight did not end there. For decades the emperors and many bishops leaned toward compromise. The man who held the line was Athanasius, who was secretary to Alexander at Nicaea and who became bishop of Alexandria in AD 328. He was exiled five times by different emperors, and is remembered with the phrase "Athanasius against the world." His book On the Incarnation argues that only God could save humanity, and that if Christ were a creature, the salvation he brought would fail. Athanasius is also the first writer known to list exactly the twenty-seven books of our New Testament, in his Easter letter of AD 367.

At the Council of Constantinople in AD 381, the Nicene Creed was expanded, in the form most churches use today, to affirm the full deity of the Holy Spirit. Arianism lingered for a while among some Germanic tribes, but the church had found the language it needed.

The twentieth century saw some of the greatest changes in the church since the Reformation. The first was the rise of Pentecostalism. A Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, in 1901 saw students speaking in tongues, and in 1906 a revival at a former church on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, led by the African American preacher William Seymour, drew worshipers of every race and spread across the world. Within a century Pentecostal and charismatic Christians numbered hundreds of millions, concentrated in Latin America, Africa and Asia.

A second change was the movement toward Christian unity. Missionaries had seen how absurd it was to export Western divisions to the mission field, and in 1910 a great missionary conference in Edinburgh began a series of efforts that led to the founding of the World Council of Churches in 1948. Evangelicals met at the Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization in 1974 and set out a common vision.

A third was the Second Vatican Council, which Pope John XXIII opened in 1962 and which ended in 1965 under Paul VI. It allowed the Mass to be celebrated in local languages, encouraged Catholics to read the Bible, said that other Christians are brothers and sisters in Christ, and affirmed religious freedom. It marked the end of centuries of hostility between Catholics and Protestants, and today they cooperate in many ways, while serious differences remain.

The century also brought severe persecution. In the Soviet Union, China, and many other places, thousands of Christians were imprisoned or killed, and by some estimates the twentieth century saw more Christian martyrs than all earlier centuries together. Yet the church survived, and in places grew. Jesus' prayer in John 17, "that all of them may be one," is still being answered in part, but not completely.

By the late seventeenth century, many Lutheran and Reformed churches in Germany had become dry, caught up in doctrinal quarrels while ordinary believers felt little warmth. In 1675 a Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt named Philipp Jakob Spener published Pia Desideria, "Pious Desires," a proposal for reform. He wanted small groups to meet for Bible study and prayer, lay people to share in the work of the church, and practical Christian living to count as much as correct belief. His movement was called Pietism.

His follower August Hermann Francke built a great complex at Halle, in Germany, with an orphanage, schools and a mission center, supported by faith and gifts. Pietism emphasized personal conversion, devotion and care for the poor, and it sent missionaries to India and elsewhere.

The most influential outgrowth was the Moravian community. In 1722 persecuted Protestants from Moravia found refuge on the estate of Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf in Saxony, who let them build a village that they called Herrnhut. In 1727 the community experienced a profound spiritual renewal, and they began a round-the-clock prayer meeting that went on for more than a hundred years. In 1732 they sent out their first missionaries to the slaves of the Caribbean, and the Moravians soon became the first large Protestant missionary movement.

Their influence reached further than their size. John Wesley met Moravians on a ship to Georgia in 1735 during a storm, and was impressed by their calm, and Peter Böhler later helped him toward the faith he sought. Pietism and the Moravians changed Protestant Christianity by showing that the heart and the head belong together, and that mission is the work of the whole church.

The Greek word martys means witness, and in the early church it came to mean someone who bore witness to Christ with their life. Accounts of martyrs were collected and read aloud, and two of the earliest are especially vivid.

Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna, a city of Asia Minor, and he had known the apostle John, according to Irenaeus. In about AD 155 or 156, when he was an old man, he was arrested during a festival. The proconsul urged him to swear by the emperor and curse Christ, and promised to release him. Polycarp answered, "Eighty-six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" He was put to death, and the account of it, written by his church in the form of a letter, is one of the oldest Christian documents outside the New Testament.

Perpetua was a young noblewoman of Carthage in North Africa, about twenty-two years old, with a baby at the breast. She was arrested in AD 203 with several others, including a slave woman named Felicity, for being a catechumen, which means a new convert preparing for baptism. Her prison diary is the earliest surviving writing by a Christian woman. In it she describes her father's pleading that she give up her faith, the dreams she had in prison, and her calm answer to him that she could be called nothing other than what she was, a Christian. She and her companions were killed in the arena.

The stories were not told to glorify death. They were told to show that the faith was worth more than life and that the Lord kept his people. The church honored the martyrs' graves, and the date of death was celebrated as their birthday into the life to come.

Jerome was born around AD 347 in what is now Croatia and educated in Rome. He was a brilliant and difficult man, an ascetic with a sharp tongue, who spent years in the Syrian desert and then in Rome as secretary to Pope Damasus. For the church of his time, his great work was the translation of the Bible into Latin.

Latin versions already existed, collectively called the Old Latin, but they were uneven and varied from place to place. In AD 382 Damasus asked Jerome to prepare a standard text. Jerome began with the Gospels, and later moved to Bethlehem, where he lived in a monastery for the last thirty-four years of his life. There he did something that no Christian scholar had done before. He learned Hebrew and translated the Old Testament directly from the Hebrew, rather than from the Greek Septuagint. He completed the work around AD 405.

His translation was eventually called the Vulgate, from the Latin for "common," and it was the main Bible of western Christendom for more than a thousand years. Many of the phrases that entered English came through it. The Council of Trent in 1546 declared it the authoritative Latin text for the Catholic Church.

Jerome made enemies, and he was criticized for translating from Hebrew and for calling some of the books of the Septuagint apocryphal. He also left a famous line that every Bible student should remember: "Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ." He is the patron saint of translators, and his work is a reminder that the Bible has always needed to be put into the language of the people who read it.

Nicaea settled that the Son is fully God. But it left the question of how to speak of one God in three persons. The answer was worked out in the later fourth century by three friends from Cappadocia, in what is now central Turkey: Basil of Caesarea, his younger brother Gregory of Nyssa, and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus.

Their contribution was largely a matter of vocabulary. The word ousia, being or substance, would name what the three share. The word hypostasis, person or subsistence, would name what each is distinctively. So God is one ousia in three hypostases. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit, yet all three are fully the one God. The three differ not in power or goodness but in their relations: the Father is unbegotten, the Son is begotten from the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

Basil also wrote On the Holy Spirit, defending the Spirit's full divinity, and used the church's own worship as evidence: the Spirit is glorified together with the Father and the Son. Gregory of Nazianzus, nicknamed "the Theologian," gave five great sermons on the Trinity, and Gregory of Nyssa wrote on how the soul grows toward God.

They also showed that theology is done on one's knees. Their works are full of prayer and wonder, and they insist that God is greater than any words can say. The result, in the creed of Constantinople in AD 381, was the formula the church still uses. And all three, Basil in particular, were also pastors who built hospitals and cared for the poor in a time of famine.

The Catholic Church did not stand still while Protestantism grew. In the sixteenth century it carried out its own internal reform, sometimes called the Counter-Reformation, and the better term is the Catholic Reformation, because many of its changes had begun before Luther.

The central event was the Council of Trent, which met in three phases between 1545 and 1563. It answered the Protestants point by point. It affirmed that Scripture and tradition together are the sources of revelation and that the Latin Vulgate is the authoritative text. It taught that justification involves inward renewal and cooperation with grace, and not faith alone. It confirmed seven sacraments and the doctrine of transubstantiation. It also reformed abuses: bishops had to live in their dioceses, seminaries were set up to train priests, and the sale of indulgences was curbed.

New orders arose, the most important of which was the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, founded by a Spanish soldier, Ignatius of Loyola, and approved by the pope in 1540. They emphasized education, discipline and mission, and opened schools and universities across Europe. Francis Xavier, one of the first Jesuits, carried the gospel to India, Southeast Asia and Japan. Teresa of Avila and John of the Cross, Spanish mystics, renewed the life of prayer in the Carmelite order.

Catholic reform also fed a flowering of art and music in the baroque era, and a vast missionary expansion into the Americas, Africa and Asia. The result was that the church held Southern Europe, and Europe was left divided between Catholic and Protestant lands. Both sides fought a series of terrible wars, ending with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which in Germany alone had killed millions in the Thirty Years' War.

The history of the church and slavery is painful, because Christians were on both sides, and each side cited the Bible. For centuries many Christians owned slaves and defended the practice, often by pointing to the regulation of slavery in the Old Testament and to Paul's instruction that slaves obey their masters. Slave ships sailed under Christian flags, and ministers preached to slaveholders. At the same time, the strongest voices for abolition were also Christian, and they drew on the Bible too.

John Newton, a slave ship captain, was converted after a violent storm in 1748, and later became a clergyman and wrote the hymn "Amazing Grace," published in 1779. Late in life he publicly repented of his part in the trade. William Wilberforce, an evangelical Member of Parliament, led the campaign to end the slave trade through some twenty years of defeats, until the Slave Trade Act of 1807, and the bill to abolish slavery itself was moving through Parliament when he died in 1833. He worked with a circle of friends known as the Clapham Sect, and with Quakers who had opposed slavery from the beginning.

In America, the enslaved people themselves transformed Christianity. They heard in the story of the exodus a promise of their own deliverance, and they sang it in the spirituals. Richard Allen, a freed slave who had been pulled from his knees in prayer at a white church in Philadelphia, founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816. The black church became a center of community life and later of the civil rights movement.

The lesson of this history is not just about the past. The same Bible was read in opposite ways, and the difference was often what the readers wanted to hear. Christians now almost universally agree that slavery is a sin, citing texts such as Paul's statement that in Christ there is neither slave nor free. The episode is a caution to read Scripture humbly, and with an ear for those who suffer.

The first generation of the church is the best documented, because Luke tells the story in Acts and the apostles wrote the letters that fill the rest of the New Testament. By the time Paul reaches Rome around AD 60, congregations of Jews and Gentiles had been planted across the eastern Mediterranean, in cities such as Antioch, Ephesus, Corinth and Philippi, and Christianity was already known to the authorities in Rome as a movement distinct from Judaism.

The Roman historian Tacitus records the first state action. In AD 64 a great fire destroyed much of Rome, and Nero, who was rumored to have started it, blamed the Christians. Tacitus says they were arrested in large numbers, and some were torn by dogs or burned as torches at night. Early tradition holds that both Peter and Paul were killed in Rome in the aftermath, though the New Testament does not tell us. Their graves were honored from very early on.

In AD 70 the Romans crushed the Jewish revolt, and the temple in Jerusalem was burned. This was an enormous event for the young church. Jesus had foretold that not one stone of the temple would be left on another (Mark 13:2), and Christians took the destruction as a sign that the old system of sacrifice had given way to the new. The church in Jerusalem, according to a tradition recorded by Eusebius, had left the city for Pella before the siege.

By the end of the century the apostles had mostly died. John, according to tradition, lived the longest, in Ephesus, and wrote his Gospel, letters and Revelation late in life. Christians now spread through the empire as a community with no temples, images or priests of the kind the Romans knew. They met in homes. They refused to sacrifice to the emperor. And as they grew, they came to be seen as a danger, and sometimes as an enemy, by the world around them.

In 1095 Pope Urban II spoke at Clermont in France, calling on the knights of Europe to help the Byzantine emperor against the Seljuk Turks and to recover Jerusalem for Christendom. The response was enormous. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in July 1099, after a siege, and the army massacred many of its inhabitants, Muslims and Jews alike. The crusaders set up several states in the Levant, which lasted for about two centuries.

Many more crusades followed, and they went badly. The Second Crusade failed in 1148. Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, though he treated its people more mercifully than the crusaders had. The Fourth Crusade turned aside in 1204 to sack the Christian city of Constantinople. The so-called Children's Crusade of 1212 ended in disaster. The last crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291. Crusading ideas were also used against heretics in Europe, such as the Cathars, and against pagans in the Baltic.

Historians still debate the motives. Many crusaders were sincere, and they believed they were doing penance and defending fellow Christians. Others were drawn by land, loot or adventure. The crusades lie at the center of Muslim memory of Christian aggression, and the Eastern church remembers 1204.

The church's own sources contain a challenge to the whole enterprise. Jesus told Pilate that his kingdom was not of this world, so that his servants would not fight (John 18:36), and told his disciples to love their enemies. Today most Christians regard the crusades as a grave failure to follow him. A story of faith should be honest about this part. The church has been the source of great good and also of great harm, and it is part of the Christian understanding of sin that this includes its own members.

When the persecutions ended and the church became popular, some Christians felt that the cost of discipleship was being lost. They went out into the desert. The movement began in Egypt in the late third century, and its first great figure was Antony, born about AD 251, who sold his property after hearing Jesus' words to the rich young man and went to live alone in the wilderness. He lived there for about twenty years and was said to have fought with demons. People began to seek him out, and his life, written by Athanasius, spread the ideal across the Christian world.

Others tried a different pattern. Pachomius, a former soldier, founded around AD 320 the first communal monastery, where monks lived together under a common rule of prayer, work and obedience. Basil of Caesarea wrote rules for monastic life in the East, and in the West the greatest was written by Benedict of Nursia, who around AD 529 founded the monastery of Monte Cassino in Italy. His Rule is short, practical and balanced, organized around the daily round of worship and work, and it shaped monastic life in the West for a thousand years.

The monks left a deep legacy. They kept learning alive through the collapse of the western empire, copying manuscripts of the Bible and many classical authors. They opened hospitals and hospitality. They became missionaries. Their sayings, collected as the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, are short and sharp and still read today.

The movement had its excesses, such as extreme self-denial, and the Reformers later criticized the idea that monks had a higher spiritual calling than other believers. But in an age when many Christians were drifting toward comfort, the monks asked what it truly costs to follow Christ.

In the seventh century a new faith appeared that changed the map of the Christian world. Muhammad, born in Mecca about AD 570, taught that there is one God and that he himself was the last of the prophets. After his death in 632, the Arab armies that followed him carried Islam outward with extraordinary speed. They took Damascus in 635 and Jerusalem in 637. Alexandria fell in 641, and by about 720 Muslim rule stretched from Spain to Persia.

Some of the oldest Christian lands were affected. The churches of Syria, Egypt and North Africa, which had produced Athanasius, Cyril and Augustine, came under Muslim rule. In most places Christians were allowed to keep their faith as a protected minority, with legal limits and an extra tax, and the churches survived, but they shrank over the centuries. Today the Coptic Church in Egypt still numbers in the millions.

Christians first met Islam as a challenge to explain themselves. John of Damascus, who served at the Muslim court in the early eighth century before becoming a monk, wrote the first Christian response, defending the Trinity and the deity of Christ. Later in the Middle Ages the contact included both warfare and scholarship, because Arabic translations of Greek philosophy came back to the Latin West through Spain and Sicily.

What later became a long history of conflict and exchange began as a question of faith. Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet but deny that he is the Son of God, that he died on the cross and that God is a Trinity, and these remain the points on which the two faiths part. Christians are asked by Peter to be ready to give a reason for their hope with gentleness and respect, and the long encounter has taught the church how hard that can be.

The generation after the apostles is called the apostolic fathers, writers of the late first and early second century who were taught by the apostles or their followers. Their writings are not Scripture, but they show what the earliest Christians believed and how they lived.

Clement of Rome wrote a long letter to the church at Corinth around AD 96, urging them to restore elders they had removed from office. He cites the Old Testament and some of Paul's letters, and speaks of the apostles appointing leaders in each church. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was arrested and taken to Rome to be executed about AD 110. On the way he wrote seven letters, urging unity around the bishop and insisting against some who said that Christ only seemed to have a body that he truly suffered and rose. The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is a short church manual that may date from the first century. It describes baptism, fasting, the Lord's Supper and two ways, a way of life and a way of death.

Another work, the Epistle of Barnabas, and the Shepherd of Hermas, both read in some churches, were eventually left out of the New Testament. Polycarp wrote to the Philippians, and Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, collected sayings about Jesus and gave some of the earliest testimony to the origin of Mark and Matthew.

These writers show a church that was already worshiping Christ as God, meeting weekly on Sunday, baptizing, sharing the Lord's Supper and holding to the apostles' teaching. They also reveal the first challenges: false teaching about the person of Christ, and splits within the community. As the eyewitnesses died, the question grew sharper: how can the church be sure of what the apostles taught? The answers came in the second century, in the form of the Scriptures, the creed and the bishops.

In the 1730s and 1740s a wave of religious revival swept through the English-speaking world, known in America as the Great Awakening. It began in the congregation of Jonathan Edwards, a pastor in Northampton, Massachusetts. In 1734 and 1735 many people in his town became deeply concerned about their souls. Edwards, who was an acute thinker and wrote with great care, described what he saw in A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God.

The revival took off with the arrival of George Whitefield, a young Anglican preacher from England with a powerful voice, who toured the colonies from 1739 to 1741, preaching outdoors to crowds of thousands. Benjamin Franklin, who did not share his beliefs, calculated that Whitefield could be heard by about thirty thousand people at once. The effect spread across denominations and colonies, and people from different backgrounds heard the same message of new birth.

Edwards's most famous sermon, "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," preached in Enfield, Connecticut, in July 1741, is often remembered for its imagery of judgment. But he was a theologian of the beauty of God, and his writings on religious affections and on the true marks of a work of the Spirit remain valuable. The Awakening also had a downside: it divided churches between those who welcomed the revival and those who resisted it, and it produced some extremes.

A second wave, the Second Great Awakening, came after 1800, with camp meetings such as the one at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, in 1801. Together, the awakenings reshaped American Christianity. They made personal conversion central, they helped Baptists and Methodists become the largest denominations, and they fed a wave of mission, education and social reform.

The Christian church began as one, and the divide between East and West came slowly. The two halves of the old empire spoke different languages, Greek in the East and Latin in the West, and had grown apart in culture and politics. After the western empire fell, the Pope of Rome came to claim an authority over the whole church, while the patriarchs in the East saw him as the first among equals. Disputes accumulated over the centuries.

One concerned a clause in the Nicene Creed. In the West the phrase "and the Son," in Latin filioque, was added to the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, first in Spain in the sixth century. The East objected, both to the theology and to a change made to the creed without a council of the whole church. Other differences concerned the use of leavened or unleavened bread in the Lord's Supper, the marriage of priests and the pope's claim to universal power.

The break is dated to 1054, when a papal legate, Cardinal Humbert, laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople against the patriarch Michael Cerularius, and the patriarch responded in kind. It was not seen as final at the time, and contact continued. But the Fourth Crusade, in 1204, when western soldiers sacked Constantinople, left a bitterness that has lasted. The mutual excommunications were formally lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras, but the churches are still not in full communion.

Today the Eastern Orthodox Church, with some 200 to 300 million members, and the Roman Catholic Church, with some 1.3 billion, remain separate. Jesus prayed that his followers might be one (John 17:21), and the division is still a wound.

When King James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, the Puritans asked him for a new translation of the Bible. At a conference at Hampton Court in 1604 he agreed. The Geneva Bible, the favorite of the Puritans, had marginal notes that he disliked, and the official Bishops' Bible was not widely loved. He appointed about fifty scholars, in six companies working at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge, to produce a version that all could use.

The translators were told to follow the Bishops' Bible and to consult the earlier English versions, and they drew heavily on Tyndale's work. Their method was careful. Each scholar translated a portion alone, then the company reviewed it together, and finally a small committee checked the result. The preface they wrote describes the aim of putting the word into a language the people could understand. The book was printed in 1611.

It took some decades to displace the Geneva Bible, but then it became the Bible of the English-speaking world for three centuries. Its cadence entered the language, in phrases such as "the skin of my teeth," "a still small voice," and "the powers that be." Its rhythm shaped English prose, poetry, and oratory. It is still loved for the beauty of passages such as the twenty-third Psalm, and by many for its dignity in worship.

Later discoveries of older manuscripts, and changes in English, led to many new translations, beginning with the Revised Version of 1881. The King James Version rested on a Greek text, the Textus Receptus, drawn from a handful of late manuscripts, and scholars now have much earlier ones. But the 1611 Bible remains one of the great works of English, and the hope of its translators, that ordinary people might read God's word, has been widely realized.

Around 1455 a goldsmith in Mainz named Johannes Gutenberg finished printing a Bible in Latin using movable metal type. Before that, every book had to be copied by hand, which could take a monk a year or more to copy a Bible. Now hundreds of copies could be produced, and printing spread through Europe faster than almost any technology before or since. By 1500 there were presses in over 250 towns.

The Bible was the first great book to be printed, and the effect on the church was enormous. In 1516 the Dutch scholar Erasmus published the first printed edition of the Greek New Testament, with his own Latin translation beside it, which showed readers where the Vulgate differed from the Greek. Erasmus wrote in the preface that he wished that the Scriptures were translated into every language, so that the farmer at his plow and the weaver at his loom could read them. His Greek text was the basis of Luther's German translation and of the English New Testament of Tyndale, and eventually of the King James Version.

Ideas moved quickly now. Luther's writings were printed and sold in the thousands within weeks. Pamphlets, sermons, hymnbooks and catechisms flowed from the presses. The Reformation was the first great movement to be spread by the printed word.

The press made the Bible possible for ordinary readers. It also began a new problem that the church is still working through: when everyone can read, who decides what the text means? That question became the central argument of the next century.

The word Puritan began as an insult for English Protestants who wanted to purify the Church of England of what they saw as leftovers of Rome. Over time it came to describe a movement as much about the spiritual life as about church order. The Puritans stressed Bible reading, preaching, careful self-examination and a disciplined life in which every ordinary task was done for God, whether farming, trade or family duty.

They suffered for their convictions. Under James I and Charles I many were fined, imprisoned or driven from their pulpits. Some left. A group of separatists who had settled in Holland sailed on the Mayflower to Plymouth in 1620. A much larger Puritan migration followed from 1630 to Massachusetts Bay, where their governor John Winthrop spoke of the colony as "a city on a hill." Those colonies laid the foundations of much of New England.

At home the Puritans won power in the Civil War of the 1640s. The Westminster Assembly of divines, which met in London from 1643 to 1649, drew up the Westminster Confession of Faith in 1646 and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms in 1647. The Shorter Catechism begins with the question "What is the chief end of man?" and answers, "Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever." These documents became the standard of Presbyterian churches around the world.

Puritan writers left a body of devotional literature that is still read today, including John Owen, Richard Baxter and Thomas Watson. John Bunyan, a tinker who spent years in Bedford jail, wrote The Pilgrim's Progress, published in 1678, which became one of the best-selling books in English. The Puritans had faults, including harshness and, at times, intolerance, but they also taught the church to take holiness and the whole of life seriously.

Luther, Zwingli and Calvin all kept some link between church and state, and all baptized infants. A group of younger men in Zurich who had studied with Zwingli concluded that this did not follow Scripture. They argued that the church should be a community of voluntary believers and that baptism belonged only to those who confess faith. On 21 January 1525 Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock in a private home, and then Blaurock baptized others. Their opponents called them Anabaptists, "re-baptizers," since they had all been baptized as infants.

The movement spread quickly and was fiercely persecuted, by Catholics and by Protestants alike. Felix Manz, one of the founders, was drowned in the Limmat River in Zurich in 1527, by the authorities of a city that called itself reformed. Thousands were killed over the next decades. Early leaders drew up the Schleitheim Confession in 1527, which called for adult baptism, separation from the world, the refusal to swear oaths and a rejection of the sword.

Most Anabaptists were peaceful, but in 1534 a group took over the German city of Münster and tried to set up a violent, apocalyptic kingdom, which was crushed the next year. That episode damaged the reputation of the entire movement for generations. The peaceful tradition was gathered by a Dutch priest, Menno Simons, whose followers became the Mennonites. Others became the Hutterites and the Amish.

Their descendants include the Mennonites, Brethren, and in some respects the Baptists, who arose in England in the early seventeenth century. Their heritage, in the ideas of believers' baptism, religious freedom, and the separation of church and state, has spread much more widely than their numbers would suggest. Many Christians who are not Anabaptist have learned from their emphasis on following Jesus' teaching about peace and about the cost of discipleship.

The first three centuries were not a constant bloodbath. Persecution was local and sporadic for most of the time. It flared up under particular emperors and governors, and for long stretches the church was left alone. But the danger was real, and the reasons for it are worth understanding.

The Romans were tolerant of foreign religions as long as they did not threaten public order and as long as their followers also honored the gods of the state. Christians refused. They would not sacrifice to the emperor, whom many Romans treated as divine, or join in the civic festivals, since these involved idols. Neighbors accused them of atheism, because they had no images, and of immorality, because of rumors about their secret meetings and the language of "eating the body" and "love feasts." Merchants who sold idols or sacrificial meat lost business. And whenever there was a flood, famine or plague, people were quick to say that the gods were angry at the Christians.

A famous letter around AD 112 shows how it worked. Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, wrote to the emperor Trajan to ask what to do about Christians. He had been questioning those accused, letting those who denied the faith go if they offered wine and incense to the emperor's image, and executing those who refused. He reported that they met before dawn to sing a hymn to Christ "as to a god," and to bind themselves by an oath not to steal, commit adultery or break their word. Trajan replied that Christians should not be hunted out, but those who were accused and refused should be punished.

The first empire-wide persecution came under Decius in AD 250, who ordered every citizen to sacrifice and obtain a certificate. The Great Persecution under Diocletian, from AD 303, was the last and the most severe, and ended with the toleration decree of Galerius in 311. Tertullian told the authorities that "the blood of Christians is seed," and in fact the church grew.

At the end of the eighteenth century, most Protestants did not think of sending missionaries overseas. Some argued that the Great Commission had been given only to the apostles. A shoemaker and Baptist pastor in England changed that. William Carey, born in 1761 in a village in Northamptonshire, taught himself Greek, Hebrew and Latin while mending shoes, and he kept a map of the world on the wall of his workshop.

In 1792 he published An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens, and preached a sermon that is summed up in the line "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God." That year the Baptist Missionary Society was formed. In 1793 Carey sailed with his family to India. He was there for forty years and never returned home.

The early years were hard. His son died of dysentery, his wife suffered a mental breakdown, and it was seven years before his first convert. But Carey worked on. He translated the Bible, in whole or in part, into dozens of Indian languages, founded a college at Serampore, campaigned against the burning of widows, and wrote grammars and dictionaries. Others followed: Adoniram Judson to Burma in 1813, Robert Morrison to China in 1807, Robert Moffat and David Livingstone to Africa, and Hudson Taylor, who founded the China Inland Mission in 1865 and urged missionaries to dress like the people they served.

The nineteenth century is sometimes called the great century of Christian missions. The work was often mixed up with Western colonial power, and missionaries made mistakes. But many of them gave their lives, brought the Bible to peoples who had no written language and opened schools and hospitals. Their work is the reason that Christianity is now a global faith.

In April 1521 Luther was summoned to the imperial assembly, called the Diet, at Worms, before the young emperor Charles V. His books were laid out on a table and he was asked whether he would take back what he had written. After a night's reflection he answered that unless he was convinced by Scripture or by plain reason, he would not recant, for his conscience was captive to the word of God. According to a printed account, he ended with the words "Here I stand. I cannot do otherwise." Scholars doubt that he said the last sentences, but they agree about the refusal.

The emperor declared him an outlaw. On his way home, friends of the Elector of Saxony pretended to kidnap him and took him to the Wartburg Castle, where he hid for ten months disguised as a knight called Junker Jörg. There he did the work that probably affected Germany more than any other: he translated the New Testament from Greek into German in about eleven weeks. It was printed in September 1522, and thousands of copies sold. He and his colleagues completed the whole Bible in 1534.

His German was vivid and plain, taken from the speech of ordinary people, and his translation did much to shape the written language itself. He insisted that the Bible should be in the language of the plowman, and he loved the idea that every Christian could read it. He married Katharina von Bora, a former nun, in 1525, and the Lutheran parsonage became a model for the family life of the pastor. He wrote hymns, including "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God." He died in 1546, in the town where he was born. The Reformation had already spread beyond his control.

By the fourteenth century many in the church felt that it needed reform. The popes had spent seventy years in Avignon in France, and then from 1378 there were two and sometimes three rival popes. The clergy were often wealthy and poorly educated, and the Bible was available only in Latin to most. In this setting, two men raised their voices.

John Wycliffe was an English scholar at Oxford, born around 1330, who argued that Scripture, and not the pope, is the supreme authority, and that every Christian should be able to read it. He attacked the sale of indulgences and some teachings about the Lord's Supper. He inspired the first complete translation of the Bible into English, made from the Latin Vulgate in the 1380s by him and his followers. His followers, the Lollards, were persecuted. He died in 1384 of natural causes, but in 1428 the church had his bones dug up and burned.

Jan Hus was a Czech priest and professor in Prague, who was influenced by Wycliffe's writings and preached in the language of the people. He was summoned to the Council of Constance in 1414 with a promise of safe conduct, and was arrested. He refused to recant what he believed to be true and was burned at the stake on 6 July 1415. His followers, the Hussites, fought for years, and some became the Moravian Church. According to one tradition, he said before his death that a goose, which is the meaning of "Hus" in Czech, would be roasted, but that a swan would come after him who could not be silenced. Many later saw Luther as the swan.

Wycliffe has been called the Morning Star of the Reformation. Both men believed that ordinary people needed the Bible in their own language, and that conviction would soon be carried by a new invention.

At almost the same time as Luther's movement in Germany, another stream of reform arose in the Swiss cities. Huldrych Zwingli, a priest in Zurich from 1519, began to preach straight through the Gospels and then through the New Testament, applying it to the life of the city. He rejected practices he could not find in the Bible, such as fasting rules and images in churches, and he was killed in 1531 in a battle between Protestant and Catholic cantons. His death left the work to others.

John Calvin was a French lawyer's son born in 1509, who studied humanities and law in Paris and underwent what he called a sudden conversion. In 1536, aged twenty-six, he published the first edition of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, a clear, orderly statement of Protestant belief that he went on to revise until the final edition of 1559. That same year the reformer Guillaume Farel persuaded him to stay in Geneva, from which he was expelled in 1538 and recalled in 1541. He was a pastor, a teacher of pastors and a writer of commentaries on most of the Bible.

Geneva became a model city and a school for reformers from across Europe, including John Knox, who took its pattern back to Scotland. Calvin taught that God's glory is the end of everything, that salvation is wholly by grace, and that the whole of life is lived before God. His followers are called the Reformed. They produced the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563 and later the Westminster Confession, and their churches are now found in Presbyterian, Reformed and many other denominations.

Calvin also has a dark side in the story. In 1553 Geneva executed the Spanish physician Michael Servetus for denying the Trinity. Calvin agreed with the verdict, though he asked for a less cruel death than burning. Even those who honor Calvin generally regard this as a failure of the age that he shared. The chief lesson is that reform of belief is not the same as reform of the heart.
